title: Ajaccio to Les Invalides: Napoleon and the Weight of Europe
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Corsica, Ponte Novu, the fall of Paoli
stops.campa: On the bridge over the Golo at Ponte Novu the last army of free Corsica breaks under French guns. Pasquale Paoli's militia, in which Carlo Buonaparte has ridden as aide, is scattered; the general sails for exile in England within the month. Three months before his second son is born, Carlo makes his peace with the conquering crown, accepts a place among the island's new French nobility, and carries his pregnant wife Letizia, who followed the army on muleback through the mountains, home to Ajaccio. The cause is lost before the boy who will avenge and betray it draws breath.
suggested_refs: The monument at Ponte Novu on the Golo
Pasquale Paoli's flight to England, June 1769

stops.name: Ajaccio, birth in the Casa Bonaparte
stops.campa: Letizia Bonaparte, hearing mass at the cathedral of Ajaccio, is seized with labor and walks the few steps home; she gives birth, the family will say, on a sofa covered in an old tapestry of Homeric heroes, so quick was the child in coming. He is christened Napoleone, for a great-uncle, in the Casa Bonaparte on the day of the Assumption. Carlo, lawyer and gentleman of modest estate, and Letizia, nineteen and iron-willed, will raise eight children in these rooms on the fault line between old Corsica and the new French order that has just swallowed it.
suggested_refs: The Casa Bonaparte, Ajaccio, now the Musée national de la Maison Bonaparte

stops.name: Brienne-le-Château, the military school
stops.campa: A gaunt, friendless Corsican boy of nine arrives at the Royal Military School of Brienne, one of twelve founded by Louis XVI for the sons of poor nobility. He speaks French badly, is mocked for his island accent and his given name, and withdraws into mathematics, geography, and the history of Plutarch's great captains. He excels at maps and siege-craft, is made a corporal of the model battalion the boys drill with, and dreams, his sister will remember, of leading Corsica back to Paoli's cause. Five years of ploughing through Latin buy him, at the end, a gift for guns.
stops.quote: I lived like a bear, in a little cell of my own... I looked upon my comrades with a species of indignation.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's recollections of Brienne, recorded by Bourrienne and Las Cases
suggested_refs: The Musée Napoléon at Brienne-le-Château, on the site of the school
The model battalion drill-ground
sources: napoleon.org, 'Napoleon Bonaparte, student of the Royal Military School in Brienne'
Las Cases, Memorial of Saint Helena

stops.name: Paris, the École Militaire, the commission
stops.campa: At the École Militaire on the Champ de Mars, in the year after his father's death leaves the family in want, the sixteen-year-old cadet sits the examinations of the artillery corps: the one branch of the service where mathematics outweighs birth. He places forty-second of fifty-eight candidates, the only Corsican in his year to pass at all, and is commissioned second lieutenant in La Fère regiment. He leaves Paris within days for the garrison at Valence, a friendless young officer with a library card, a subscription to Rousseau, and no fortune but his slide-rule.
suggested_refs: The École Militaire on the Champ de Mars, Paris

stops.name: Ajaccio, the break with Paoli, exile of the family
stops.campa: The Revolution has split Corsica as it has split France. Paoli, restored to power and now suspect to Paris, breaks with the young officer's family when brother Lucien denounces him before the Convention; the Bonapartes are declared enemies of the Corsican cause and their house is sacked by a mob. Napoleon, his mother, and his sisters flee down to the harbor by night and take ship for Toulon with almost nothing saved. He lands in France a refugee of twenty-three, stripped of the island loyalty that shaped him, with only the Revolution left to serve.
suggested_refs: The sack of the Casa Bonaparte, June 1793
Pasquale Paoli's declaration against the Bonaparte family

stops.name: Toulon, the siege, the artillery command
stops.campa: At the siege of royalist, English-held Toulon the wounded chief of artillery is replaced by a twenty-four-year-old captain recommended by his fellow Corsican Saliceti. Bonaparte lays out the batteries himself, walks the guns under fire, has a horse shot from under him, and takes a bayonet wound in the thigh. His plan, to seize the promontory of L'Éguillette and drive the British fleet from the roads with converging fire, succeeds in a single night's assault; Hood's ships stand out to sea, and Toulon falls. The representatives promote him brigadier general at twenty-four, over guns pointed correctly for the first time in his life.
suggested_refs: Fort l'Éguillette, the 'Batterie des hommes sans peur' at Toulon
Bonaparte's promotion to brigadier general, December 1793

stops.name: Paris, 13 Vendémiaire, the guns before Saint-Roch
stops.campa: The Convention, threatened by a royalist rising of the Paris sections, hands its defense to Barras, who calls on the unemployed Corsican general idling in the capital. Bonaparte sends Murat racing for the cannon parked at the Sablons before the insurgents can seize them, and lines his guns along the rue Saint-Honoré and the steps of the church of Saint-Roch. When the columns of the sections advance he opens with grapeshot at point-blank range; the crowd breaks and scatters within minutes. The Convention is saved, the phrase 'a whiff of grapeshot' enters the language for it, and Barras remembers the name of the gunner.
suggested_refs: The church of Saint-Roch, rue Saint-Honoré, still pocked with the grapeshot of 13 Vendémiaire

stops.name: Paris, marriage to Joséphine
stops.campa: At the mairie of the second arrondissement, past ten at night, the twenty-six-year-old commander of the Army of Italy marries Rose de Beauharnais, six years his elder, widow of a guillotined vicomte, mother of two, and mistress lately of the all-powerful Barras. He signs the register giving himself an extra year and her a few less; witnesses include Barras himself. Two days later he leaves for the front without her, and begins from the road the flood of letters that will call her Joséphine: the name he has already decided suits her better than her own.
stops.quote: I awake full of you. Your image and the intoxicating pleasures of last night have left no rest to my senses... Sweet and incomparable Joséphine, what a strange effect you have upon my heart!
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Joséphine, December 1795 – March 1796 (Correspondance de Napoléon Ier)
suggested_refs: The marriage register at the mairie of the 2nd arrondissement, rue d'Antin
Napoleon's love letters to Joséphine

stops.name: Lodi, the bridge
stops.campa: At the long wooden bridge over the Adda at Lodi, Austrian guns rake the crossing at point-blank range. Bonaparte forms columns of grenadiers under the parapet, out of the line of fire, and leads the charge himself among his generals, sword in hand, into the smoke; the bridge is carried and the rear guard broken. That night, walking the field, he first feels, he will tell Bourrienne years later, the ambition of executing great things stir in him as more than a fantastic dream. His soldiers, admiring the gunner who still sights his own cannon, begin calling him le petit corporal.
stops.quote: It was not till after Lodi that I saw myself as a superior being, and conceived the ambition of performing great things which so far had filled my thoughts only as a fantastic dream.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon, recorded by Bourrienne, Mémoires
suggested_refs: The bridge of Lodi over the Adda
The nickname 'le petit corporal'
sources: the-past.com, 'Lodi and Arcola: making the myth'

stops.name: Arcole, the flag on the bridge
stops.campa: Against the Austrians relieving Mantua, the army stalls before the narrow causeway and bridge at Arcole, swept by artillery from the far bank. When his infantry balk, Bonaparte seizes a tricolor standard himself and runs onto the dike in the open, calling the grenadiers to follow their general; his aide Muiron falls dead at his side shielding him, and he is pulled back into the marsh, nearly drowned, by his own staff. The bridge is not taken that hour, but the image, the general with the flag under fire, outruns the fact and becomes, within the year, the Republic's most reproduced picture.
stops.quote: Grenadiers, come and seek your colour!
stops.quote_source: General Augereau at the bridge of Arcole, 15-17 November 1796; Bonaparte repeats the act with a second flag
suggested_refs: Antoine-Jean Gros, Bonaparte au pont d'Arcole (1801)
The obelisk at Arcole (1810) commemorating the flag

stops.name: Campo Formio, the treaty, Venice given away
stops.campa: At the château of Campo Formio, negotiating with imperial Austria on his own authority and largely against his government's instructions, twenty-eight-year-old General Bonaparte dictates the peace of a continent. Austria cedes the Austrian Netherlands and recognizes French dominion in Italy; in exchange, Bonaparte hands over the thousand-year republic of Venice, never conquered by him and occupied only by trickery months before, as a coin of the settlement. He returns to Paris a peacemaker and a name greater than the Directory that employs him, having taught Europe that a general in the field can make its treaties.
stops.quote: The Republic of Venice has no other title than that of a conquest which I have made.
stops.quote_source: Bonaparte, letter justifying the cession of Venice, 1797 (Correspondance)
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Campo Formio, 17 October 1797
The fall of the Venetian Republic, May 1797

segments.name: Egypt: the Savants and the Sphinx

stops.name: Alexandria, the landing
stops.campa: Slipping past Nelson's fleet in fog and luck, the expedition of five hundred ships lands its army on the beach west of Alexandria. Bonaparte reads his soldiers a proclamation promising respect for Islam and the Prophet, casting the invasion as liberation from the Mamluk beys rather than conquest of Egypt; few of the exhausted, thirst-maddened troops who storm the walls that same night believe a word of it, but the words themselves, printed also in Arabic, announce a new kind of European war, fought as much with printing presses and savants as with bayonets.
stops.quote: Peoples of Egypt, you will be told that I have come to destroy your religion; do not believe it... I respect God, his Prophet, and the Qur'an more than the Mamluks do.
stops.quote_source: Bonaparte's proclamation to the Egyptians, 2 July 1798
suggested_refs: Bonaparte's proclamation to Egypt, printed in French and Arabic
The walls of Alexandria, stormed 2 July 1798
sources: Wikipedia, 'French campaign in Egypt and Syria'

stops.name: Giza, the Battle of the Pyramids
stops.campa: Within sight of the pyramids of Giza the army forms its divisions into hollow squares, artillery and baggage sheltered within the ranks, to receive the charge of Murad Bey's Mamluk cavalry: the most magnificent horsemen Bonaparte's soldiers have ever faced, in cloth of gold, sabres flashing, each rider a small treasury of arms. The squares hold; disciplined volley fire breaks charge after charge, and the Mamluks are driven into the Nile or the desert. Legend will put in the general's mouth, gesturing at the monuments across the river, the sentence that outlives the battle's true tactics by far.
stops.quote: Soldiers, from the summit of these pyramids, forty centuries look down upon you.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Bonaparte before the battle, first printed by Gourgaud in 1823, likely a later legend rather than words spoken on the field
suggested_refs: The Great Pyramids of Giza, backdrop of the battle
The Mamluk cavalry of Murad Bey
sources: shannonselin.com, 'Napoleon at the Pyramids: Myth versus Fact'

stops.name: Cairo, the founding of the Institut d'Égypte
stops.campa: In a requisitioned Cairo palace Bonaparte founds the Institut d'Égypte on the model of the Institut de France, and takes his own seat not as commander but as an ordinary member, under the presidency of the mathematician Monge. Berthollet, the naturalist Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, the artist Denon, and a hundred and fifty savants measure the Sphinx and survey the temples of Karnak and Luxor, founding the modern study of ancient Egypt in the months before Nelson's fleet, one August night, burns the transport ships at anchor in Aboukir Bay and seals the army inside the country it has just begun to read.
suggested_refs: Description de l'Égypte (1809-1829)
The Institut d'Égypte's measurements of the Sphinx
sources: napoleon.org, 'The Institut d'Égypte and the Description de l'Égypte'
lindahall.org, digital exhibition on Napoleon in Egypt
Wikipedia, 'French campaign in Egypt and Syria'

stops.name: Acre, the failed siege
stops.campa: Before the walls of Ottoman Acre, defended by the Turkish governor and the British commodore Sidney Smith with guns taken from Bonaparte's own captured siege train, the march north out of Egypt breaks. Two months of failed assault, plague among the wounded, and no breach; Bonaparte visits the pest-house himself, they say, and touches the dying to steady his men. He lifts the siege and marches the wreck of the army back across the desert to Egypt, his first campaign ended in outright failure, and confides to his staff the empire of the East he might have built had this one town fallen.
stops.quote: If I had been able to take Acre, I would have put on a turban... I would have made myself emperor of the East, and I would have returned to Paris by way of Constantinople.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon, recorded conversation on Saint Helena
suggested_refs: The walls of Acre (Akko), still standing
Sidney Smith's defense of Acre, 1799

stops.name: Fréjus, the return to France
stops.campa: Abandoning the army he commands to Kléber without leave of the Directory that sent him, Bonaparte slips past the British blockade in two frigates and lands at Fréjus to a welcome no defeated general fleeing his own war should expect: church bells, crowds unhitching his carriage horses to draw it themselves, bonfires along the road to Paris. The Republic he finds on his return is bankrupt, invaded on every frontier, and ruled by a Directory that has burned through its credit with the nation. Egypt already forgotten, all France seems to be waiting only to be told what to do next, and by whom.
suggested_refs: Bonaparte's landing at Fréjus, 9 October 1799
The crowds that greeted him on the road to Paris
sources: napoleon.org, '18 Brumaire: context and course of a coup'

stops.name: Saint-Cloud, the 18 Brumaire
stops.campa: Moved on a pretext to the palace of Saint-Cloud, away from the Paris mob, the two legislative councils meet under the guard of Bonaparte's own soldiers. In the Orangerie the deputies of the Five Hundred, sensing the trap, mob him physically, tear his coat, and shout him outlaw; he is white and shaking when his brother Lucien, president of the council, saves the coup by declaring falsely that deputies had drawn daggers on the general. Murat's grenadiers clear the hall at bayonet-point, and by night three Consuls rule France in place of five Directors. The Revolution, Bonaparte tells the nation, is over.
stops.quote: Citizens, the Revolution is fixed upon the principles which began it. It is ended.
stops.quote_source: Bonaparte's proclamation of 19 Brumaire, Year VIII (10 November 1799)
suggested_refs: The Orangerie of Saint-Cloud, scene of the coup
The Constitution of the Year VIII

stops.name: Marengo, lost at five, won at seven
stops.campa: Surprised by the Austrian army of Melas near the farmhouses of Marengo, the First Consul's forward divisions are driven back all morning, and by five in the afternoon the battle looks lost, the field littered with French dead and stragglers streaming to the rear. Then General Desaix's division, recalled at a gallop, strikes the disordered Austrian columns in the flank; Desaix falls dead in the first charge, and Bonaparte, shown the body that evening, is seen to weep, and forbidden, by the mask of command he must wear, to weep as he wishes. The rout becomes a French victory that saves the Consulate before it is a year old.
stops.quote: I lost the battle at five o'clock; I won it back again at seven.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon, recollection of Marengo (widely cited period attribution)
suggested_refs: The farmhouse of Marengo, near Alessandria
The death of General Desaix

stops.name: Paris, the Code civil promulgated
stops.campa: After four years of drafting sessions the First Consul himself has chaired, arguing points of inheritance and contract with the jurists Portalis, Tronchet and Cambacérès late into the night, the Code civil des Français is promulgated in a single text of over two thousand articles: civil equality, secular marriage, careers open to talent, property secured, feudal privilege abolished for good. It will be carried by his armies into a dozen countries and outlast every one of his crowns. Long after Saint Helena he will say this, not Austerlitz, is the work that will not be washed away.
stops.quote: My true glory is not to have won forty battles... Waterloo will erase the memory of so many victories. But what nothing will erase, what will live eternally, is my Civil Code.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon, recorded on Saint Helena (widely cited memoir attribution)
suggested_refs: The Code civil des Français, promulgated 21 March 1804
The Conseil d'État sessions on the Code
sources: azquotes.com, Napoleon on the Civil Code

stops.name: Paris, Notre-Dame, the self-coronation
stops.campa: In Notre-Dame, before Pope Pius VII and the assembled dignitaries of the new Empire, Napoleon has the crown of Charlemagne carried to the altar, and at the moment the pontiff would set it on his head he turns, takes the crown from the tray himself, and places it on his own head before crowning the kneeling Joséphine beside him. The gesture is calculated to the inch: no priest, no king gives him this; he takes it, and Rome merely attends. Outside, cannon salute for hours and Paris roars for the new Emperor: acclaim that a young Venezuelan named Bolívar, watching from the crowd, will remember longer than the crown itself.
stops.quote: Joseph, if our father could see us now!
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to his brother Joseph during the coronation, 2 December 1804 (recounted in period memoirs)
suggested_refs: Jacques-Louis David, Le Sacre de Napoléon (1807)
The crown of Charlemagne used in the ceremony
bolivar.journey.json (the coronation watched from the crowd, shared pin)
sources: napoleon.org, 'A close-up on the coronation of Napoleon I'

segments.name: The Zenith of the Grande Armée

stops.name: Milan, the Iron Crown
stops.campa: In the Duomo of Milan, six months after Notre-Dame, Bonaparte crowns himself a second time: King of Italy now, with the ancient Iron Crown of the Lombard kings, said to be forged from a nail of the True Cross. He lifts it from the altar himself, as at Paris, and sets it on his own head before the assembled notables of the new kingdom, pronouncing the old Lombard warning aloud. Days later, at the grand review on the plain outside the city, a young traveler from Caracas named Bolívar watches the Emperor ride past within arm's reach amid the blaze of his marshals, and studies the little man in grey the way a rival studies a rival.
stops.quote: God gives it to me; beware whoever touches it.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon at his coronation as King of Italy, Milan, 26 May 1805 (the traditional Lombard formula, per period accounts)
suggested_refs: The Iron Crown of Lombardy, Monza cathedral treasury
Andrea Appiani's portraits of Napoleon as King of Italy
bolivar.journey.json (Bolívar watching the review, shared witness)

stops.name: Austerlitz, the sun
stops.campa: On the first anniversary of his coronation, on the frozen Pratzen heights near the little Moravian town of Austerlitz, Napoleon lures the combined armies of Austria and Russia, the two emperors watching from the field themselves, into abandoning the high ground, then strikes the weakened center with Soult's divisions out of the morning mist as, famously, the sun breaks through. Sixteen thousand Allied dead and prisoners against under nine thousand French; the Third Coalition is broken in a single day. His soldiers will remember 'the sun of Austerlitz' for the rest of their lives as the luckiest light that ever rose on them.
stops.quote: Soldiers, I am pleased with you... it will be enough for you to say, 'I was at the battle of Austerlitz,' for people to reply, 'There is a brave man.'
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's proclamation to the army after Austerlitz, 3 December 1805
suggested_refs: The Pratzen Heights, Austerlitz battlefield
'The sun of Austerlitz', invoked in later proclamations
sources: napoleon.org, 'a rather pale Sun of Austerlitz'

stops.name: Jena-Auerstedt, Prussia broken in a day
stops.campa: On a single October day the two wings of the Grande Armée shatter the army of Frederick the Great's heirs at Jena and at Auerstedt twelve miles apart: Napoleon commanding the larger action without even realizing, until evening, that Davout's single corps has alone destroyed the main Prussian army at Auerstedt while the Emperor merely mopped up a secondary force at Jena. Fortresses that held Frederick's cannon surrender without firing a shot; the King and Queen of Prussia flee to the Russian frontier. On the very plateau where the philosopher Fichte had once lectured on the free self, the old Prussian state ceases, for years, to exist as more than a name on French maps.
suggested_refs: The battlefield plateau of Jena-Auerstedt (14 October 1806)
Davout's III Corps at Auerstedt
fichte.journey.json (the philosopher's Jena, shared ground)

stops.name: Bayonne, the Spanish Bourbons abdicate
stops.campa: At the château of Marracq outside Bayonne, having lured both Spanish claimants across the frontier under promise of arbitration, Napoleon extracts the crown from father and son in three days: on the fifth of May Charles IV renounces the throne to him outright; that same day, not yet knowing of his father's act, Ferdinand VII abdicates in Charles's favor, unwittingly signing the crown straight through to the French Emperor. Napoleon hands Spain, a nation he has never troubled to understand, to his brother Joseph within the week: the single act, more than any battle, that teaches all Europe the word guerrilla and opens the wound that never fully closes.
suggested_refs: The Château de Marracq at Bayonne
The Abdications of Bayonne, 5-7 May 1808
sources: san_martin.journey.json (Bailén, the first defeat of Napoleon's eagles)

stops.name: Erfurt: Voilà un homme, the meeting with Goethe
stops.campa: At the Congress of princes he has summoned to Erfurt to overawe his ally the Tsar, Napoleon takes an hour from kings to receive the German poet whose Werther he has read seven times and carried through Egypt. He studies Goethe and pronounces, before witnesses, the sentence that will outlive most of the treaties signed that week, "there is a man," then turns the talk to tragedy, faults the drama of fate as belonging to a darker age, and urges him to write of Caesar instead. He leaves Goethe the cross of the Legion of Honor, still master of every crowned head in the room.
stops.quote: Voilà un homme!
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Goethe at Erfurt, 2 October 1808 (as Goethe records it)
suggested_refs: Kaisersaal, Erfurt, site of the audience
goethe_full.journey.json (the shared Erfurt pin)

segments.name: The Marriage of Empires and the Russian Catastrophe

stops.name: Wagram, the hundred-gun battery
stops.campa: On the marshy plain of Wagram, north of Vienna, in the second and decisive day of battle against the Archduke Charles, Napoleon masses Macdonald's massive infantry column and a battery of a hundred guns under Lauriston in the center, the largest concentration of artillery the wars have yet seen, and blasts a gap through the Austrian line. It is a costlier, cruder victory than Austerlitz: over thirty thousand French casualties in two days, but it forces Austria's fifth and last war against him to an end at the peace of Schönbrunn, clearing, at ruinous cost, the ground for the dynastic marriage he has already begun to plan.
suggested_refs: Macdonald's column and Lauriston's hundred-gun battery at Wagram
The Treaty of Schönbrunn, October 1809

stops.name: Paris, divorce from Joséphine
stops.campa: In the small salon of the Tuileries, before the assembled family, Napoleon reads a prepared statement dissolving fourteen years of marriage for reasons of state alone: Joséphine has given him love and years of happiness, he says, but no heir, and the Empire he has built needs a womb of undisputed royal blood to outlast him. Joséphine, weeping, tries to read her own reply and cannot finish it; he embraces her before the room. She keeps the title of Empress, the château of Malmaison, and his continuing, oddly tender letters, but the throne beside him is already being measured for an Austrian archduchess.
stops.quote: The interest of France... the good of the state, which desires that I leave behind me children who inherit my love for my people, requires that I renounce henceforth the sweetest connections of my life.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's statement of divorce, read to the imperial family, 15 December 1809
suggested_refs: The Tuileries salon of the divorce ceremony
Château de Malmaison, Joséphine's retreat

stops.name: Paris, marriage to Marie-Louise
stops.campa: Married by proxy in Vienna to an Austrian archduchess he has never met, a niece by marriage of blood to the Marie-Antoinette whose fall he witnessed as a cadet in the Paris crowds, Napoleon receives his eighteen-year-old bride at Compiègne and, by his own account, cannot wait for the religious ceremony to consummate the match. The public wedding, in the Salon Carré of the Louvre transformed into a chapel, seats every crowned head and ambassador he can summon; the House of Habsburg he once studied from the outside as a rival empire now supplies, by treaty of the bedchamber, the legitimacy his own crown was still missing.
suggested_refs: The Salon Carré of the Louvre, chapel for the wedding
The proxy marriage in Vienna, March 1810

stops.name: Paris, birth of the King of Rome
stops.campa: After a labor so dangerous the doctor Dubois is authorized, if it comes to a choice, to save the mother over the child, Marie-Louise delivers a son at the Tuileries. The cannon salute is arranged in advance to announce the sex: twenty-one shots for a daughter, a hundred and one for a son, and all Paris counts with the guns; at the twenty-second the whole city erupts before the salute is even finished. Napoleon carries the infant himself to the doors of the state apartments, presents him to the assembled grandees of the Empire with four words, and gives him, by decree already prepared, the title no Bonaparte has ever held: King of Rome.
stops.quote: Here is the King of Rome.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon presenting his newborn son, 20 March 1811 (period court memoirs)
suggested_refs: The Tuileries Palace, site of the birth (destroyed 1871)
The title 'Roi de Rome' created for Napoleon II
sources: shannonselin.com, 'The Perilous Birth of the King of Rome'
napoleon.org, 'The Roi de Rome, son of Napoleon I'

stops.name: Moscow, entry and the fire
stops.campa: After Borodino's slaughter, the bloodiest single day the wars have yet produced, the Grande Armée enters an undefended, half-emptied Moscow, and Napoleon takes the Kremlin, "I am at length, then, in Moscow, in the ancient city of the Tsars," expecting Alexander's surrender within days. Instead the governor Rostopchin has seeded the city with incendiaries; that night fires break out across Moscow and within days more than two-thirds of the wooden capital burns to ash around the French garrison, lighting the Kremlin walls red by night. Napoleon watches from a window and calls it the most magnificent and frightening sight mankind has ever seen; the surrender he waited for never comes.
stops.quote: What resoluteness! What people! These are Scythians!
stops.quote_source: Napoleon, on learning Moscow's own governor had ordered the city burned, September 1812 (recorded by Ségur and other memoirists)
suggested_refs: The Kremlin, entered 14 September 1812
The Fire of Moscow, 1812
sources: smithsonianmag.com, 'these retreating soldiers burned down their own city'

stops.name: Berezina, the crossing
stops.campa: Five weeks into the retreat from a Moscow that gave him ashes instead of peace, the wreck of the Grande Armée, starved, frostbitten, shadowed by Cossacks, finds the Berezina unfrozen and both banks held by converging Russian armies. General Éblé's pontonniers stand chest-deep in the freezing current for hours, building two trestle bridges under fire, and hold the crossing open two full days while a hundred thousand men, camp-followers, and guns funnel across; when the bridges are finally burned behind the rearguard, thousands still on the wrong bank are lost. The army that crossed the Niemen in June is, by the time it reaches Poland, a scattered fraction of itself.
suggested_refs: Éblé's pontoon bridges at Studzianka
The Retreat from Moscow, painted by January Suchodolski and others
sources: historyhit.com, 'How Dutch Engineers Saved Napoleon's Grand Armée'

stops.name: Leipzig, the Battle of the Nations
stops.campa: Half a million men, French against the combined armies of Austria, Prussia, Russia and Sweden, meet at Leipzig in the largest battle Europe has yet fought, four days of slaughter that cost some hundred and thirty thousand casualties before Napoleon, his Saxon allies deserting on the field itself, orders retreat across the single bridge over the Elster. A panicking corporal blows the bridge too soon, with thirty thousand French rearguard still on the wrong side; among the drowned is the Polish marshal Poniatowski, made marshal only days before. It is the Empire's largest defeat yet, and the war rolls, for the first time since 1794, onto French soil.
suggested_refs: The premature destruction of the Elster bridge, 19 October 1813
The drowning of Marshal Poniatowski

stops.name: Fontainebleau, farewell to the Old Guard
stops.campa: In the Cour du Cheval-Blanc at Fontainebleau, having failed a night before to end his own life with a phial of poison carried since Russia, Napoleon comes down the horseshoe staircase to say goodbye to the men who followed the eagles for twenty years. He kisses the tricolor of the Old Guard's standard, embraces General Petit, and tells the ranked grenadiers, most of them weeping openly, some fainting in the ranks, that he goes for the good of France, to spare her a civil war his own continuance would prolong. The Allies have already voted him the tiny island of Elba as sovereign; the Bourbons return to a throne he leaves them.
stops.quote: Soldiers of my Old Guard, I bid you farewell. For twenty years you have been my constant companions on the road to honour and glory... I could not embrace you all, but I embrace your general. Come, General Petit, let me press you to my heart.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's farewell to the Old Guard, Fontainebleau, 20 April 1814
suggested_refs: The horseshoe staircase (escalier du Fer-à-Cheval) at Fontainebleau
The eagle standard of the Imperial Guard
sources: napoleon.org, 'Napoleon's adieux to the Old Guard at Fontainebleau'
Wikisource, 'Napoleon I's speech following his abdication'

stops.name: Elba, exile
stops.campa: Sovereign now of nothing but a Mediterranean island eighteen miles long, granted by the Allies as a face-saving cage, Napoleon governs Elba as if it were an empire in miniature: he reorganizes its mines, its roads, its tiny army of four hundred, redesigns his gardens at the Palazzina dei Mulini, and receives his mother and his sister Pauline while Joséphine, whom he still writes of with feeling, dies at Malmaison without his knowing until after. He reads the Vienna newspapers that reach him late, watches the Bourbon restoration mishandle a France already restless, and counts, from his window over the sea, the days until the money the treaty promised him stops arriving.
suggested_refs: The Palazzina dei Mulini, Napoleon's residence on Elba
The tiny army of the principality of Elba
sources: shannonselin.com, 'How did Napoleon escape from Elba?'

stops.name: Golfe-Juan, the flight of the eagle
stops.campa: With six hundred men of his Elba garrison packed onto a handful of small ships, Napoleon slips past the British watch and lands, without a shot fired, on the beach at Golfe-Juan between Cannes and Antibes. He avoids royalist Provence and strikes north through the mountains toward Grenoble, issuing along the road the proclamation drafted on shipboard, promising his soldiers that the eagle, with the national colors, will fly from steeple to steeple all the way to the towers of Notre-Dame. Near Laffrey a royal battalion blocks the pass; he walks alone toward their muskets, opens his coat, and dares them to fire on their Emperor. They break ranks and cheer him instead.
stops.quote: Soldiers! ... The eagle, with the national colours, will fly from steeple to steeple, all the way to the towers of Notre-Dame.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's proclamation to the army, 1 March 1815
suggested_refs: The landing beach at Golfe-Juan
The confrontation at Laffrey, near Grenoble, 7 March 1815
The Route Napoléon

stops.name: Waterloo, the last battle
stops.campa: On the muddy ridge of Mont-Saint-Jean, having failed to crush the Prussians decisively at Ligny two days before, Napoleon delays his main attack until the ground dries and gives Blücher's army the hours it needs to march to Wellington's aid. Ney's cavalry breaks itself for hours against unbroken British squares; the Imperial Guard, sent forward at last in the evening as the final reserve of twenty years of war, is thrown back for the first time in its history, and the cry that the Guard recoils breaks the whole army's nerve. Napoleon is swept from the field in the general rout, his last throw of everything spent by nightfall against Wellington and the Prussians together.
stops.quote: The Guard recoils... All is lost.
stops.quote_source: Cries reported through the French ranks as the Imperial Guard broke, evening of 18 June 1815 (period accounts of the rout)
suggested_refs: The ridge of Mont-Saint-Jean, Waterloo battlefield
The repulse of the Imperial Guard, evening of 18 June 1815
sources: shannonselin.com, 'What did Napoleon say about the Battle of Waterloo?'

stops.name: Longwood, arrival on Saint Helena
stops.campa: After a second abdication in Paris and two months of British custody aboard the Bellerophon and the Northumberland, Napoleon lands on Saint Helena, a volcanic speck in the South Atlantic chosen for its total isolation, and is housed at Longwood, a damp, rat-infested former cattle farm two thousand feet above the sea. Governor Hudson Lowe restricts his movements, opens his mail, and insists on addressing him only as 'General Bonaparte'; Napoleon, in return, refuses most invitations from a jailer he will not dignify with courtesy. He plants a garden, dictates history to whoever will write it down, and settles, at forty-six, the master of Europe eleven months before, into the last exile.
stops.quote: I would rather be a poor peasant in a country cottage than a king kept like me.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon at Longwood, recorded conversation (Las Cases, Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène)
suggested_refs: Longwood House, Saint Helena
Governor Hudson Lowe's restrictions on Napoleon

stops.name: Longwood, Las Cases and the Memorial
stops.campa: In the small damp rooms of Longwood the comte de Las Cases, chamberlain and interpreter, begins the daily discipline that will become the Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène: hours of dictation on the campaigns, the Consulate, the Code, and the theory of war, taken down each evening and copied fair by his own son. Napoleon shapes, sentence by sentence, the account of himself that will outlive the Bourbon restoration and the Bourbon histories written against him: the Revolution's heir, not its gravedigger; the liberator of peoples, not their conqueror. Las Cases is deported by Lowe within the year for smuggling letters, but the notebooks travel with him, and the legend they contain reaches Paris years before the body does.
stops.quote: We will write our Memoirs.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Las Cases, aboard the Bellerophon, August 1815, on the purpose of exile
suggested_refs: Las Cases, Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène (1823)
Longwood House, site of the dictation

stops.name: Longwood, the death of the Emperor
stops.campa: After months of wasting illness, stomach pain, vomiting, a decline his doctors misread almost to the end, Napoleon dictates a will dividing his modest fortune among his family and old soldiers, asks that his ashes rest on the Seine among the French people he loved, and dies at Longwood in the late afternoon, a violent storm breaking over the island at the hour of his death. Witnesses who lean close to catch his last words hear only fragments: France, the army, head of the army, and, some swear, Joséphine's name at the very end. He is buried, at Lowe's insistence, under an unmarked stone in the Sane Valley.
stops.quote: France, l'armée, tête d'armée... Joséphine.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's last words, variously recorded by attendants at Longwood, 5 May 1821
suggested_refs: The unmarked grave in the Sane Valley, Saint Helena, 1821-1840
Napoleon's last will and testament
sources: jrmccarthy-law.com, 'Last Will & Testament of Napoleon Bonaparte'

stops.name: Les Invalides, the retour des cendres
stops.campa: Nineteen years after Longwood, on the initiative of minister Thiers, eager to borrow the dead Emperor's glory for a shaky monarchy, the frigate Belle Poule, commanded by the Prince de Joinville, carries the exhumed and startlingly well-preserved body home across the winter Atlantic. Through a snowstorm the gilded funeral chariot, drawn under the Arc de Triomphe and down the Champs-Élysées, brings the coffin to the Dôme des Invalides before six hundred thousand Parisians massed in the cold: the eagle's flight completed at last, the towers of Notre-Dame outdone by the dome under which he will lie, twenty years dead and, the crowd senses, not at all finished with France.
stops.quote: I desire that my ashes may repose on the banks of the Seine, among the French people whom I have loved so well.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's will, Longwood, 1821, the wish fulfilled by the retour des cendres, 1840
